USS Missouri. The last Iowa-class battleship, which served as the flagship where Japan formally surrendered on September 2, 1945, ending World War II in the Pacific. Her decks became the setting for history's most momentous naval ceremony, symbolizing American naval dominance and the conclusive defeat of Japan.

Missouri was commissioned in 1944 and arrived in the Pacific just in time to participate in the bombardment of Japanese homeland targets in the war's final months. She hosted the formal Japanese surrender ceremony on September 2, 1945, with General Douglas MacArthur and Admiral Chester Nimitz presiding as Japanese officials signed the Instrument of Surrender. This single event gave her an outsized place in American collective memory of World War II's conclusion.

After the war, Missouri served throughout the Cold War and Korean War, later modernized with missile systems and radar, extending her operational life well into the 1950s and beyond. She was decommissioned in 1955 but retained in reserve, eventually becoming a museum ship berthed in Pearl Harbor and later in Missouri, where she remains a major tourist attraction. Known affectionately as "Mighty Mo" by her crew, her participation in the surrender ceremony made her the symbolic capstone to the Pacific War. Her presence at Japan's formal capitulation in 1945 furnished the literal stage for one of the twentieth century's pivotal moments, and the most advanced capital ship design of World War II continues to embody that historic endpoint.
